claims.claim: Unsafe medication practices and medication errors are a leading cause of injury and avoidable harm in health care systems worldwide, and errors can occur at different stages of the medication use process — prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administration, and monitoring.
Medication errors occur when weak medication systems and/or human factors such as fatigue, poor environmental conditions, or staff shortages affect the medication use process.

In the United States, medication errors affect more than 7 million patients and result in approximately 7,000 to 9,000 deaths each year, with medical costs exceeding $40 billion — figures that count only reported cases (Tariq et al., 2023, cited in OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills chapter 11).
About half of medication errors occur during the medication ordering process, and nurses and pharmacists identify 30 to 70 percent of medication-ordering errors before they reach the patient.

The five core rights of medication administration are right patient, right drug, right route, right time, and right dose; the American Nurses Association (2021) recommended adding right reason, right documentation, and right response.

The five core rights are confirmed at three checkpoints — when the medication is obtained, when it is prepared, and when it is administered at the bedside — with the medication label compared to the medication order at each checkpoint.

The right-patient check uses two or more patient identifiers (such as full name and date of birth) confirmed by the patient, the wristband, or an agency-approved method; the right-drug check includes comparing the label to the order, checking the expiration date, and confirming patient allergies.

High-alert drugs are drugs that can cause significant harm if an error occurs — examples include insulin, anticoagulants, chemotherapy drugs, and opioids — and hospitals add safeguards such as two-nurse verification, restricted access in automated dispensing cabinets, and tall-man lettering on similar drug names.

When a drug administration error occurs, actual or potential, it should be reported immediately according to the agency's policy; an actual error requires close monitoring of the patient and documentation of the response, while a potential error is reported because it educates the team and allows interventions to prevent a future actual error.

Patients can help prevent medication errors by knowing their medicines, keeping a written list of everything they take (including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbs) plus their allergies, reading medication labels every time, and asking their provider or pharmacist questions such as why they are taking a medicine.

WHO launched Medication Without Harm, the third Global Patient Safety Challenge, on 29 March 2017 in Bonn, Germany, aiming to reduce severe avoidable medication-related harm by 50 percent globally; its key action areas are polypharmacy, high-risk situations, and transitions of care.

WHO lists medication errors among the common sources of preventable harm in health care and incident reporting for learning and continuous improvement among the organized activities of a safe health system.

positions: Five core rights (right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time) per OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills section 11.1.
The American Nurses Association (2021) recommends adding right reason, right documentation, and right response.
Some curricula and texts extend the list further (right education, right of refusal, right history and assessment).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the five core rights as the standard floor and presents the additions explicitly as evidence that the rights are a floor, not a complete system — no single list is presented as exhaustive.

positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills (citing Tariq et al., 2023) reports more than 7 million U.S. patients affected and roughly 7,000-9,000 deaths per year, plus costs exceeding $40 billion.
WHO estimates the global cost of medication errors at $42 billion USD annually.
All figures undercount because they depend on reporting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the OpenStax-reported U.S. figures with the explicit caveat that they count only reported cases; no invented precision and no unsourced dollar figures in the lesson prose.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft framed medication safety as 'a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations' with only two generic subsections (The core idea; How to reason with it) and no factual claims or sources. Nothing in the draft survived review; the lesson was rebuilt from source-verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate with a six-subsection, source-verified lesson.
Added the WHO-attributed working definition (practices that prevent medication errors across the medication use process) and the systems-and-human-factors framing.
Added the honest framing that the five rights are a floor, supported by the ANA additions and the ordering-stage error data.
Added original worked examples (Renaldo's three checks; Mrs. Delgado's penicillin allergy) not present in the draft.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills, Section 11.1: Rights of Medication Administration (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (per this subject's source-map). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; book published June 26, 2024). Supports: the five core rights (right patient, right drug, right route, right time, right dose); the ANA 2021 additions (right reason, right documentation, right response); the three checkpoints (obtaining, preparing, bedside administration) with label-to-order comparison at each; right-patient identification via two or more identifiers; allergy confirmation as part of the right-drug check and the pre-administration assessment; questioning doses outside the safe range; consulting the provider for route changes; high-alert drugs (insulin, anticoagulants, chemotherapy, opioids) with safeguards; tall-man lettering; ~75% of medication errors associated with distractions and interruptions roughly every two minutes (ISMP 2012); reporting actual and potential errors immediately per agency policy; right of refusal. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
